Eastern red scorpionfish (Scorpaena cardinalis) is a relatively small-bodied scorpaenid endemic to temperate rocky reefs. Analysis of long-term field surveys indicates that the maximum recorded total length reaches 40.5 centimeters [Li = 40.5 centimeters], a size that positions this species at the smaller end of the size spectrum within the genus. This ultimate length is accompanied by a corresponding maximum adult wet weight of 1780 grams [Wwi = 1780 grams], a value derived from the length-weight relationship established for the population. The gonadosomatic index (GSI) averages approximately 3% [GSI = approximately 3%] when measurements were taken at a water temperature of 17 °C [T = 17 °C]. The protracted growth trajectory implied by this size suggests a species that prioritizes somatic persistence over rapid biomass turnover.

Reproductive development in female Eastern red scorpionfish follows a pattern common among slow-growing scorpaenids. Histological examination of ovarian tissue indicates that the total length at which 50 percent of females attain puberty is 22 centimeters [Lp = 22 centimeters], a threshold estimate consistent with values reported for the congeneric species Scorpaena scrofa. This length corresponds to roughly 54 percent of the ultimate total length, a proportion that may reflect an energetic trade-off between achieving a size sufficient to support egg production and the need to begin reproduction before senescence reduces fecundity. Field observations of gravid females suggest that individuals below this size rarely exhibit vitellogenic oocytes, reinforcing the 22 centimeters [Lp = 22 centimeters] length as a reliable indicator of the onset of sexual maturation. This length-at-puberty represents a critical life-history parameter informing the minimum size limit for any future management considerations.

The early life stages of Scorpaena cardinalis are characterized by a brief embryonic period followed by the emergence of a yolk-sac larva. Incubation trials conducted at a stable temperature of 17.6 °C [T = 17.6 °C] demonstrated that hatching occurs after 14 days [ab = 14 days], a duration comparable to that reported for other temperate scorpaeniform species. The newly emerged yolk-sac larva carries an initial wet weight of approximately 0.0018 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0018 grams], a mass that reflects the modest egg diameter of around 1.5 millimeters typical of this family. During the subsequent lecithotrophic phase, the prolarva relies exclusively on endogenous yolk reserves, progressively absorbing the yolk sac over roughly one week before the mouth opens and the exotrophic transition begins. The timing of hatching at 14 days [ab = 14 days] at 17.6 °C [T = 17.6 °C] appears tightly linked to ambient temperature, as developmental rate in teleost embryos is strongly temperature-dependent.

Longevity under natural conditions has been estimated from annuli counts on otoliths collected across the species' range. The maximum documented lifespan for Scorpaena cardinalis in the wild is 33 years [am = 33 years], a value that emerged from individuals sampled at a site where mean annual water temperature approximates 17.6 °C [T = 17.6 °C]. This remarkable longevity is unusual among scorpaenids of its body size and suggests a life-history strategy centered on slow somatic growth, delayed senescence, and repeated reproductive events across multiple decades. The ultimate body size is 40.5 centimeters [Li = 40.5 centimeters]. Senescent individuals captured near the limit of this 33-year (33 years) [am = 33 years] lifespan often display worn dentition and reduced body condition at a temperature of 17.6 °C [T = 17.6 °C].

The interplay between the species' slow growth and its thermal environment is evident when comparing population parameters across different latitudinal gradients. The maximum body mass of 1780 grams [Wwi = 1780 grams] is achieved only after many years of sustained feeding on benthic crustaceans and small fishes, a diet that supports gradual mass accumulation without the need for rapid energy turnover. The gonadosomatic index of approximately 3% [GSI = approximately 3%] was recorded at 17 °C [T = 17 °C]. The age at birth of 14 days [ab = 14 days] at 17.6 °C [T = 17.6 °C] also governs the timing of larval release relative to seasonal peaks in planktonic prey abundance. Overall, the life history of Eastern red scorpionfish reflects a conservative strategy in which moderate annual fecundity and slow juvenile growth are offset by exceptional adult survivorship and a long reproductive window.
